section_title: What does the feeding reveal about Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 After this, Jesus crossed to the other side of the Sea of Galilee (that is, the Sea of Tiberias). 2 A large crowd followed Him because they saw the signs He was performing on the sick. 3 Then Jesus went up on the mountain and sat down with His disciples. 4 Now the Jewish Feast of the Passover was near. 5 When Jesus looked up and saw a large crowd coming toward Him, He said to Philip, “Where can we buy bread for these people to eat?” 6 But He was asking this to test him, for He knew what He was about to do. 7 Philip answered, “Two hundred denarii would not buy enough bread for each of them to have a small piece.”

8 One of His disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to Him, 9 “Here is a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish. But what difference will these make among so many?” 10 “Have the people sit down,” Jesus said. Now there was plenty of grass in that place, so the men sat down, about five thousand of them. 11 Then Jesus took the loaves and the fish, gave thanks, and distributed to those who were seated as much as they wanted. 12 And when everyone was full, He said to His disciples, “Gather the pieces that are left over, so that nothing will be wasted.” 13 So they collected them and filled twelve baskets with the pieces of the five barley loaves left over by those who had eaten.

14 When the people saw the sign that Jesus had performed, they began to say, “Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world.” 15 Then Jesus, realizing that they were about to come and make Him king by force, withdrew again to a mountain by Himself.

context_lines: A large crowd follows Jesus across the Sea of Galilee because of His signs among the sick. He sits on a mountainside with His disciples, and the Gospel notes that Passover is near.

Jesus asks Philip where they can buy bread for the people. This is a test; He already knows what He will do. Philip sees that even a large sum would not buy everyone a little. Andrew points to a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish, while asking what such a small amount could accomplish.

Jesus has the people sit on the grass, gives thanks and distributes the food. Everyone has as much as they want, and twelve baskets of pieces remain. About five thousand men are seated; the account does not give the exact total of everyone present.

The people recognize a sign and call Jesus the Prophet who is to come. When He realizes they intend to make Him king by force, He withdraws alone. Their response raises the question of whether they understand what kind of mission He has come to carry out.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readers commonly understand this as Jesus truly feeding the crowd and revealing His identity through the sign. Calvin also emphasizes the difference between recognizing something about Him and trying to take control of His kingship, as the crowd attempts to do. ([Calvin on John 6:14–15](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/john/6.htm))
god_plan_lines: The Passover setting places this feeding beside Israel’s memory of deliverance and God’s provision of bread in the wilderness. Later in this chapter, the crowd explicitly raises the manna account, and Jesus points to the Father’s gift of the true bread that gives life. The connection is therefore part of the Gospel’s own explanation, rather than only a similarity noticed by later readers. ([Exodus 16:1–15](https://biblehub.com/bsb/exodus/16.htm); [John 6:31–35](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/6.htm))

Another supported parallel is Elisha’s feeding of a hundred people with twenty barley loaves. His servant questions the small supply, yet the people eat and have some left over according to the Lord’s word. Jesus’ provision for the much larger crowd belongs alongside that earlier sign of God’s abundance. ([2 Kings 4:42–44](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_kings/4.htm))

The grass and the satisfying meal also recall the shepherd’s care in Psalm 23: God leads His flock to pasture and provides for them. That is a parallel with Jesus’ care here, not a claim that John quotes the psalm. The scene holds together the crowd’s actual hunger and the greater life-giving purpose that Jesus will explain. ([Psalm 23:1–5](https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/23.htm))
